newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK RATES EASE BUT SEEN CLIMBING BY END-WEEK.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK RATES EASE BUT SEEN CLIMBING BY END-WEEK.

text.p: Slovak interbank rates eased to around 20 percent on Wednesday but traders said they expected them to rebound by Friday as the end of a minimum reserve period (PMR) on August 15 nears.
Short-term deposits are still the most traded funds with overnights hovering at 20 percent and up to one-week money at 23 percent.

"Again, it will depend on whether the central bank (NBS) adds liquidity to the market...If the NBS does not add some funds, rates may go to 25 or 26 percent and could even hit 30 percent shortly before end of the reserve period," said Dalibor Cernicka, head of the Bratislava-based Money Market Broker.
Dealers said that even if the NBS adds some crown liquidity to the market, the volume was not likely to be large enough to bring about a fall in rates to below 20 percent.
"The NBS may add just as much as will be needed for banks to meet their PMR. It may be around two bilion crowns in one-week repo money," said Rastislav Zivor of ING Bank.
The fulfilment of PMR by commercial banks is one of the NBS's main yardsticks for assessing money market liquidity.
According to NBS figures, the Slovak banking sector, as of August 13, exceeded by 1.26 percent the cumulative volume of funds needed to meet PMR later this month.
High yields at Finance Ministry auctions of state paper and predictions of a further increase in these yields in coming months are likely to keep interbank rates above 20 percent, dealers said.
The ministry on Wednesday accepted an average yield of 19.926 percent at an auction of 13-week treasury bills, up from 18.248 percent in the last auction of similar T-bills on July 16.
On Tuesday it said it was drafting a new law introducing a tax on yields from state securities and that the law was expected to become effective in the fourth quarter.
Dealers said banks had already started to include the planned tax in their yield calculations of longer state securities.

"The prediction is that yields of longer state paper will be nearing the interbank rates levels and that they could rise up to 25 percent by the end of this year," said one Bratislava-based money market dealer.
